title: Face to Face Sounds
theme: Responsive sound play, face to face
materials: No materials needed — choose a calm, awake moment.
instructions: Hold or position your child comfortably so you can see each other's faces. Make one soft, simple sound such as "oooo" or "aahh," then pause for a few seconds. If your child makes any sound, respond by copying it or making your sound again. Pause and give them another chance to respond. Continue the back-and-forth for a short time while your child seems interested and comfortable.
success_criteria: The child makes any sound other than crying during at least one pause.
make_easier: Use one soft sound and repeat it once or twice before pausing. If your child looks at you, moves, or changes their expression without making a sound, treat that as engagement and keep the interaction warm, but wait for a vocal sound before counting it as vocalization success.
make_harder: Try a second simple sound, or wait for your child to make a sound first and then copy it back.
group_play_line: Another familiar person can sit nearby and take turns responding to your child's sounds.
what_to_avoid: Keep your child comfortably supported and supervised. Stop if your child looks away repeatedly, becomes unsettled, or seems tired. Do not keep prompting in order to get a sound.

title: Silly Mouth Sounds
instructions: Sit or hold your child where they can comfortably see your face. Make one playful mouth sound, such as a gentle raspberry or lip buzz. Smile, pause for a few seconds, and give your child time to respond. If your child makes any sound, vocalizes, or tries a similar mouth sound, respond warmly and make the playful sound again. Repeat for a short time while your child is interested.
success_criteria: The child makes any sound other than crying, or attempts a playful lip sound, during at least one pause.
make_easier: Choose just one gentle sound and model it a few times. Your child does not need to copy the sound. Any vocal response can count as participation in the sound exchange.
make_harder: Try two different playful sounds, such as a raspberry and a lip buzz. Pause after each one and see whether your child begins to imitate one of them or offers a different sound for you to copy.
group_play_line: A sibling or another familiar person can make one playful sound, then pause and give your child a turn.
what_to_avoid: Do not manipulate your child's lips or tongue or try to physically show them how to make the sound. Keep the sounds gentle, stop if your child turns away or seems tired or uncomfortable, and do not repeatedly prompt for imitation.

title: High and Low Sounds
theme: Exploring different voice sounds and pitches
instructions: Choose one simple sound your child already enjoys hearing, such as "ooo," "ahh," or "mmm." Make the sound once in a slightly higher voice, then once in a lower voice. Pause after each one and give your child time to respond. If your child makes any sound, copy it back or respond with one of your high or low sounds. Keep the interaction playful and brief while your child is interested.
success_criteria: The child makes any vocal sound during at least one pause, or changes the sound they make during the interaction.
make_easier: Use just one comfortable sound and repeat it without changing pitch. Pause and respond to any vocal sound your child makes.
make_harder: Alternate between two clearly different but gentle pitches, such as a higher "ooo" and a lower "ooo." You can also let your child make a sound first and then copy its pitch as closely as you can.
group_play_line: A sibling or familiar person can take turns making a high or low sound and pausing for your child to respond.
what_to_avoid: Do not try to make your child vocalize more loudly, encourage screaming, or make very loud sounds close to your child. Keep the sounds gentle and comfortable, and stop if your child startles, turns away, or seems tired.

title: Your Turn, My Turn Sounds
instructions: Make one simple sound, then pause for a few seconds and give your child time to respond. When your child makes any sound, respond by copying it or making a similar sound back. Pause again and give your child another turn. Continue the back-and-forth for a short time while your child seems interested. Think of it like a tiny conversation made of sounds.
success_criteria: The child makes at least one vocal sound during a pause and participates in at least one back-and-forth sound exchange.
make_easier: Start by listening for a sound your child makes naturally. Copy that sound back, then pause. Your child does not need to respond immediately or copy your sound.
make_harder: Try to keep the sound conversation going for several turns. Let your child start some turns, and sometimes introduce a different simple sound to see whether they respond.
group_play_line: A sibling or familiar person can join for one turn at a time, so your child hears different people responding to their sounds.
what_to_avoid: Do not fill every pause with your own sounds or repeatedly prompt your child to respond. Give them time, and stop when they look away, become unsettled, or lose interest.

title: Ba-Ba-Ba
theme: Playing with repeated sounds and early babble
materials: No materials needed; optional photo of a familiar person.
instructions: When your child is awake and interested, make one simple sound while they can comfortably see your face. You might use a single sound such as "ba," "ma," or "da," or repeat it a few times: "ba-ba-ba." Pause for a few seconds and give your child time to respond. If your child makes any sound — a vowel, squeal, babble, or syllable — respond warmly and copy their sound or repeat yours. Keep the sound play brief and enjoyable. Optional variation with people or photos: if your child enjoys looking at familiar people or family photos, use that interest during the sound game. Look at a photo together or sit near a familiar person and make a simple playful sound such as "ma-ma," "ba-ba," or "da-da." Pause and respond to whatever sound your child makes. The goal is the back-and-forth sound play, not getting the child to say the person's name.
success_criteria: The child makes any vocal sound during at least one pause. For a child who is already babbling, an attempt at a consonant-vowel sound such as "ba" or "ma" is an additional sign of progress, but it is not required for the activity to be successful.
make_easier: Use one simple vowel or sound, such as "ahh" or "ooo," rather than repeated syllables. Pause and respond to whatever vocal sound your child offers.
make_harder: Try two different syllables, such as "ba-ba" and "ma-ma," at different times. Pause before each model to give your child a chance to make a sound first. If your child begins repeating a syllable on their own, copy it back and turn it into a short sound conversation.
group_play_line: A sibling or familiar person can make one simple sound, pause, and then respond to whatever sound your child makes.
what_to_avoid: Do not repeatedly ask your child to copy or say a particular syllable. Accept the sounds they are already making and keep the interaction playful rather than treating repeated babble as a test.

title: Sounds in Our Routines
theme: Building sound play into familiar everyday routines
materials: No special materials — use a routine you already do every day, such as diaper changing, getting dressed, bath time, stroller time, or getting ready for bed.
instructions: Choose one familiar routine and one simple moment within it. At the same point each time, make a playful, gentle sound such as "ooo," "aaa," "mmm," or "ba-ba." Pause for a few seconds and give your child time to respond. If your child makes any sound, respond warmly by copying it or making your routine sound again. Use the same sound at the same part of the routine for several days so your child begins to recognize the playful pattern.
success_criteria: The child makes any vocal sound during at least one pause in the familiar routine.
make_easier: Choose just one routine and one simple sound. Model the sound once or twice and respond warmly to any vocalization your child makes. Your child does not need to copy your sound.
make_harder: Once your child recognizes the routine, pause before making the familiar sound and see whether they vocalize first. You can also introduce a second playful sound at another predictable moment in the same routine or during a second familiar routine.
group_play_line: A sibling or another familiar caregiver can use the same playful sound at the same point in the routine so the pattern stays familiar.
what_to_avoid: Do not stretch out care routines or repeatedly prompt your child in order to get a sound. Keep your child comfortably supported and supervised, and stop the sound play if they seem tired, uncomfortable, or no longer interested.

title: Peekaboo Sounds
materials: No materials needed — you can use your hands or a light cloth.
instructions: Sit where your child can comfortably see you. Briefly cover your face with your hands, then uncover it and say a playful "Boo!" Smile and pause for a few seconds to give your child time to respond. If your child makes any sound, smile, copy their sound, or say "Boo!" again. Repeat for a few rounds while your child is enjoying the game.
success_criteria: The child makes any vocal sound during at least one pause or begins to vocalize in anticipation of or after the reveal.
make_easier: Keep your face hidden for only a moment and use the same gentle "Boo!" each time. Your child does not need to copy the sound — any vocal response counts.
make_harder: Pause briefly after uncovering your face before saying "Boo!" to see whether your child makes a sound first. You can also let your child lead: if they make a sound, copy it before starting the next peekaboo turn.
group_play_line: A sibling or familiar person can take turns hiding their face and saying "Boo!" while your child watches and responds.
what_to_avoid: Keep the hiding brief and playful. Do not suddenly shout "Boo!" or try to startle your child. Stop if your child turns away, becomes upset, or no longer seems interested.
